tasks.q: Display the message Oak Lane tuck shop.
brief: Nothing is typed in by the user, and nothing else is printed.

tests.why: Nothing was printed. Text goes inside print( ) and inside quotation marks.

tasks.fb: That is a whole program: print() shows one line, and the quotation marks say where the text starts and ends.

teach.say: print() puts one line on the screen. The text goes inside the brackets, in quotation marks.

tasks.q: Ask the user for an item. Display two lines, the first Oak Lane tuck shop and the second [item].
brief: Print exactly: Oak Lane tuck shop
tasks.starter: # Print the shop name, then the item

tests.why: Only the item appeared, so the line of text is missing. Text to print goes inside print() and inside quotation marks.
input() hands back the whole line, spaces included, so both words come back as one value.
If the word item came out instead of Cheese roll, the variable was in quotation marks. Quotation marks mean print these letters.

tasks.fb: print() sends one line to the screen, and fixed text has to be inside quotation marks.

teach.say: print() shows one line of text, inside quotation marks. input() hands back whatever the user typed, and a variable holds it until you print it.
code: drink = input("Drink? ")   # the user types tea

tasks.q: Ask the user for an item. Display three lines: ===== Tuck shop ===== at the top, then [item], then Thank you.

tests.why: Count the equals signs: five, a space, Tuck shop, a space, five more.
If the word item appeared in the middle, it was inside quotation marks.
Three lines of output needs three print() statements, and they run in the order written.

tasks.fb: Each print() starts a new line, so three lines of output means three print() statements in the right order.

teach.say: Each print() makes a new line, and they run in the order you write them.

tasks.q: Ask the user for the customer's name. Keep the fixed price 90 in a constant called PRICE. Display [name], then [price] on the next line.
brief: Put the whole number 90 in a constant called PRICE. It is fixed in the program, not typed in.
tasks.starter: # Make the constant, then print the name and the price

tests.why: Two lines: the name, then the price. If the words name or PRICE appeared, they were in quotation marks.
Print the variable rather than retyping a name of your own, or only one of these tests can pass.
The 90 has to come from the constant, so the price is written down in one place only.

tasks.fb: A variable is a named box for a value. A constant is the same box for a value that must not change, and capitals are how programmers say so.

teach.say: A constant is a variable whose value never changes. Its name is written in capitals so everyone can see it must stay as it is.

tasks.q: Put the text Closed in a variable and display it. Then ask for a new message, store it in that same variable and display [message].
brief: Put the text Closed in a variable and print it.
tasks.starter: # One variable, printed twice, with a new value in between

tests.why: Closed must be printed before the variable changes. If only the new message appeared, the first print is missing.
Assigning with = throws the old value away, which is why it has to be printed first.
Both lines match here only because the new message happens to be Closed. The program still prints twice.

tasks.fb: A variable holds one value at a time, and = overwrites it.

teach.say: = replaces whatever the variable held before, so only the newest value is left. Print the old value before you overwrite it.

tasks.q: Ask the user for one word. Display [word] three times, one on each of three lines.
brief: Ask the user for one word.
tasks.starter: # Read the word, then print it three times

tests.why: Three lines exactly. One line means the value was printed once; nothing at all means input() was never stored in a variable.
input() reads the whole line, spaces included, so the full name comes back as one value.
Reading again instead of printing the variable three times will not work: there is only one line of input.

tasks.fb: input() waits for one line and hands it back. Store it once and you can use it as often as you like.

teach.say: A variable keeps its value, so you can use it as many times as you like.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a stop name and then a time. Display two lines, the first [time] and the second [stop name].
brief: Print the time, then the stop name on the next line.
tasks.starter: # Two inputs in, two lines out, the time first

tests.why: The stop arrives first but is printed second, so store each input in its own variable and then choose the order.
One input() reads one line only. Two lines of input need two separate calls.
The time is text here, not a number, so it prints exactly as it was typed.

tasks.fb: Reading and printing are separate steps. Once each value is in a variable you can print them in any order.

teach.say: One input() reads one line, so two lines need two calls. Each value goes in its own variable, and you print them in any order.
code: a = input("First? ")   # the user types red

tasks.q: Ask the user for a first name and a last name. Join them and display one line in the form [first name] [last name] is a member.
brief: Print one line: the first name, a space, the last name, a space, then exactly: is a member
tasks.starter: # Read two names, join them, print one line

tests.why: AnnaLee means the space is missing. Joining never adds spaces for you: first + ' ' + last.
Three lines instead of one means three print() statements. Build the whole sentence, then print it once.
If the word first or last appeared, it was inside the quotation marks. Only the fixed words belong in quotes.

tasks.fb: Joining text with + is called concatenation. It joins exactly what you give it, so every space is joined in on purpose.

teach.say: The + sign joins text together. It adds nothing of its own, so any space you want has to be joined in too.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a name. Display four lines: [name], then the integer 3, then the real number 0.25, then the Boolean True.
brief: Ask the user for a name, and print it.
tasks.starter: # A string, an integer, a real number and a Boolean, one per line

tests.why: 0.25 is a real number, so print the number. 0.250 or 25p or a pound sign are strings and will not match.
Four lines are wanted, and each value needs its own print().
A Boolean is written True or False with a capital letter and no quotation marks. In quotes it is only a string that looks like one.

tasks.fb: Integer, real, Boolean, character and string are the five data types OCR names, and the type decides what you can do with a value.

teach.say: Python values come in different types: 7 is an integer, 1.5 a real number, False a Boolean, and text in quotation marks a string.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Add the second to the first and display [total] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
tasks.starter: # Two whole numbers in, one total out

tests.why: 147 is the giveaway: + joined two strings instead of adding them. Wrap each one in int(input()).
Cast before adding, not after. int(input()) + int(input()) works; adding first joins the text.
A 0 is still a number to be read, so both lines must be read, in order.

tasks.fb: Casting with int() turns a string of digits into a whole number you can do arithmetic with.

teach.say: input() always hands back text, and + joins text instead of adding it. int() turns the text into a whole number first.

tasks.q: Ask the user for an amount, which may have a decimal point. Display one line in the form Fine due: [amount] pounds, with the amount as a real number, so 3 shows as 3.0.
brief: The user types in one amount, which may have a decimal point.
tasks.starter: # Read the amount, make it a real number, print the sentence

tests.why: A crash here is joining a number to text with +. Cast it back with str(fine) first.
2.50 in the sentence means the text went straight in. float() makes it a real number, and 2.50 and 2.5 are the same real number.
3 instead of 3.0 means int() was used. An integer has no decimal part; a real number always shows one.

tasks.fb: float() casts text to a real number and str() casts a number back to text. One line often needs both.

teach.say: float() turns text into a real number, which always keeps a decimal part. str() turns a number back into text so + can join it.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a name and then the whole number of races already run. Display [name] of Elm, then [races plus 1] on the next line.
brief: The user types in two lines: a name, then a whole number of races already run.
tasks.starter: # A name and a number in. Name of Elm, then one more race.

tests.why: 31 on the second line means the races were still text, so 1 was joined on the end. Cast with int() before adding.
0 races plus 1 is 1. If the second line is empty, the arithmetic is missing.
The whole typed line is the name, spaces included, and the words of Elm are joined on with +.

tasks.fb: Most programs are this shape: read the inputs, cast each one, work something out, print it in the form asked for.

teach.say: Read each value, cast it to the type you need, then print the answer in the form the question asks for.
code: team = input("Team? ")   # the user types Owls

stations.name: Final challenge: name the data type

tasks.q: Which data type would Python use for each value?
tasks.fb: Choosing the right type first saves a casting bug later on.

info.title: The first line
info.text: Printing a greeting has been the traditional first program in a new language since the 1970s.

info.title: Naming rules
info.text: A Python variable name can hold letters, digits and underscores, but it cannot start with a digit or contain a space.

info.title: Why it waits
info.text: input() reads one whole line, so the program only carries on once the Enter key has been pressed.

info.title: One bit each
info.text: A boolean has only two possible values, so it needs just one bit of storage - the smallest piece of data there is.

info.title: Silent rounding
info.text: int() on a float throws the decimal part away instead of rounding, so int(3.9) is 3.

info.title: Reading an error
info.text: A traceback names the line that failed. Read its last line first: that says what Python could not do.
